turns.text: What do you remember about your very first night after arriving in Beidahuang? What did you see, hear, and feel as you tried to fall asleep?

The first night, I lay on a narrow wooden bunk in a room that smelled of damp earth and old straw. The wind outside was relentless, rattling the window panes and slipping through every crack, so sharp it made my skin sting even under the heavy quilt. I heard the low voices of others—some crying quietly, some whispering about the work ahead. My own body was stiff from the long train ride, and my mind was crowded with the faces I’d left behind. I stared at the ceiling, tracing the lines where the boards didn’t quite meet, listening to the unfamiliar creaks of this new place. My stomach was a tight knot, not just from hunger but from the fear of the unknown. I kept my coat on, even in bed, because the cold felt like it could seep straight into my bones. I remember thinking the darkness here was thicker than in Shanghai, and I wondered how many nights it would take before I stopped counting the hours until morning.

The way you describe the cold and the darkness makes it feel so isolating. When you heard others crying or whispering that night, did you feel any urge to reach out to them, or did everyone mostly keep to themselves at first?

That first night, it felt like we were all wrapped in our own invisible shells. I could hear the girl on the bunk above me sniffling, and for a moment I thought about saying something—maybe just asking if she was alright—but the words stuck in my throat. We were strangers, thrown together only by circumstance, and I think everyone was too overwhelmed to offer comfort. It was easier to pretend I didn’t hear, to focus on my own worries. The air was thick with the sense that if you let yourself be vulnerable, you might never stop crying. So we lay there, close enough to hear each other’s breathing, but each of us alone with our thoughts. It wasn’t until much later that we started to talk to each other in the dark.

I understand that instinct to protect yourself by staying silent. You mentioned the fear of the unknown and how it kept you awake—was that fear more about the physical hardships you expected, or was it about the people in charge and the rules you’d have to follow?

It was both, but in different ways. The physical hardships were immediate and concrete—I worried about whether I could keep up with the farm work, whether I’d get enough to eat, if I’d get sick from the cold. But the fear of the people in charge was a different kind of weight. I didn’t know what would be expected of me, or how strict the rules would be. I’d heard stories back in Shanghai about people being punished for small mistakes or for not showing enough enthusiasm. That kind of fear followed me even into my dreams—I’d wake up with my heart racing, unsure if I’d done something wrong without realizing it. The uncertainty made everything feel unstable, like the ground itself could shift beneath me at any moment.

It’s striking how you describe fear as something that even followed you into your dreams. You mentioned being worried about not showing enough enthusiasm—do you remember a specific moment early on when you felt pressured to act a certain way, even if it didn’t feel genuine to you?

The first week, we were called to a meeting in the big shed after a long day in the fields. Everyone was exhausted—mud clinging to our boots, hands raw from pulling weeds. Inside, the air was thick with the smell of sweat and wet clothing. One of the leaders stood up front, pacing back and forth, his voice sharp as he talked about the “spirit” we were supposed to show. He wanted us to sing revolutionary songs—loud, with fists raised. My throat was sore from the cold, but I forced myself to sing along, louder than I felt. I watched the others, too—some eyes shining with effort, some faces empty, just moving their mouths.

Afterward, he pointed at a few people, saying they hadn’t sung with enough passion. I felt my chest tighten, worried he’d look at me next. I learned quickly to keep my face bright and my voice strong, even when I felt nothing but exhaustion. Sometimes, after those meetings, I’d step outside and feel the night air on my face, trying to remember what it felt like to act naturally, not just perform. That tension—between what I truly felt and what I had to show—never really left me.

That image of forcing yourself to sing with a sore throat while watching others do the same really stays with me. When you stepped out into the night after those meetings, did you ever talk with anyone about how fake it all felt, or was that something you kept entirely to yourself?

At first, I kept it all inside. Standing outside in the darkness, I’d sometimes catch someone else’s eye, and for a second, I’d wonder if they felt the same. But no one dared to say it out loud. We’d talk about the weather, or how hard the work was, but never about the performance itself. It was too risky—there was always the fear that someone might repeat what you said, even without meaning harm. I remember once, as we walked back to the dormitory, someone muttered under their breath that their voice was hoarse from “all this shouting.” There was an awkward silence, then nervous laughter, and the conversation quickly shifted. I realized then that we were all pretending, not just for the leaders, but for each other too. The truth was something we learned to keep hidden, even from our closest companions.

That sense of watching your words, even with people beside you in hardship, feels suffocating. Did you ever start to resent the leaders themselves, or did you see them as trapped in the same system as you? Or maybe it was more complicated than that?

It was complicated. Sometimes I’d watch the leaders—especially the younger ones—and wonder if they believed what they were saying, or if they were just as scared as we were. There were moments when I felt real anger, like when someone was singled out and humiliated for not being “enthusiastic enough.” But other times, I’d notice a flicker of hesitation in a leader’s eyes, or a sigh when they thought no one was listening. It made me think they were also performing, just with higher stakes. That realization didn’t erase my resentment, but it did make me feel a kind of pity, too. We were all caught up in something bigger than ourselves, and sometimes it was hard to tell who was really in control.

The way you describe seeing both anger and pity in yourself toward the leaders makes me wonder about moments of connection. Did you ever witness—or experience—an unexpected act of kindness or understanding from someone in authority, even if it was small or subtle?

Once, after a day when my hands were so numb I could barely hold the sickle, I was assigned to sweep the yard outside the canteen. My fingers wouldn’t close properly around the broom, and I was moving slowly, afraid someone would notice and accuse me of slacking. One of the older supervisors passed by. Usually, he kept his distance—his face always set, voice clipped. That day, he paused, glanced down at my hands, and told me quietly to go inside and warm them by the stove for a while. He didn’t say it twice, just kept walking as if nothing had happened.

Inside, I pressed my palms against the metal, feeling the sting as my skin came back to life. I looked out the window and saw him standing with the others, his posture stiff and unreadable. He never mentioned it again, and neither did I. It was a small thing, and it didn’t change my situation, but for a moment, it softened the line between us. I never forgot that brief moment of mercy, even if it was hidden under everything else.

That moment by the stove feels so fragile, like a secret shared in silence. After that, did you find yourself looking at that supervisor differently, or did you have to push the memory aside to protect yourself from disappointment?
